\paragraph{Discussion.}
For calibrated models (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B), beam search achieves DR=0\% across all four model-dataset combinations (both SciERC with 7 entity types, 551 documents, and DocRED with 96 relation types, 50 documents), regardless of schema complexity.
On SciERC, beam search eliminates DR for both Qwen (0.93\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and Llama (0.08\%\,$\to$\,0\%), and substantially reduces CF (Qwen: 9.90\%\,$\to$\,0.53\%; Llama: 6.56\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).
On DocRED (matched 50-document subsets), beam search eliminates DR for both Qwen (8.69\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and Llama (1.58\%\,$\to$\,0\%), with CF reductions of 74\% and 86\% respectively.
Llama DocRED shows the largest R-F1 gain ($+$3.4\,pp), consistent with beam search recovering valid type assignments that greedy decoding missed due to constraint fallback.
The CF reduction is an indirect effect: beam search reduces constraint-fallback frequency by exploring alternative token sequences that satisfy both grammar and semantic masks simultaneously, avoiding the fallback-to-grammar path that produces cross-field inconsistencies under greedy decoding.

Mistral-7B-v0.3 constitutes a boundary condition on both datasets.
On SciERC (7 entity types), beam search does not reduce DR (13.4\%\,$\to$\,13.8\%), though CF drops by 55\% relative (1.27\%\,$\to$\,0.57\%) and R-F1 improves by $+$0.7\,pp; the unchanged DR confirms that all residual violations stem from entity type misclassification, not constraint-search failure.
On DocRED (96 relation types), beam search reduces DR by 25\% relative (28.4\%\,$\to$\,21.4\%): the more complex schema introduces constraint-search failures that beam exploration resolves, but the entity misclassification component remains.
This contrast reveals that beam search resolves constraint-search failure (where greedy decoding encounters $G(t) \cap S(t) = \emptyset$ conflicts) but cannot overcome fundamental model calibration limitations in entity typing.

\paragraph{Runtime overhead.}
\label{sec:runtime}
S1 overhead is $+$13.1\% on SciERC, lower on DocRED due to amortization over longer sequences; under LoRA, $+$10.0\% with 37\% lower absolute latency.
Constraint compilation is one-time $<$0.5\,s; scaling benchmarks confirm constant overhead (2--3\%) up to 200 entity types and 1{,}000 relations (Appendix~\ref{app:scalability}).

\paragraph{Beam search compatibility.}
\label{sec:beam-results}
% exp_id: d066_beam_sweep
With LoRA, beam search~\cite{anderson2017guided} eliminates all four violation types on both SciERC and DocRED at both 8B and 70B scales (Appendix~\ref{app:beam-search}).
A beam-width sweep ($k \in \{1,2,4,8\}$) on SciERC reveals $k{=}2$ as Pareto-optimal: R-F1 44.60 (highest), CF 0.11\%, at only 1.18$\times$ greedy latency; $k{=}4$ achieves CF${=}$0\% but lower R-F1 (43.60) at 1.39$\times$ latency (Table~\ref{tab:beam-latency}).
This yields three deployment tiers: greedy S1 ($+$10\% latency, DR${<}$0.1\%, CF${\leq}$1.4\%), beam $k{=}2$ (1.18$\times$, near-zero CF), and beam $k{=}4$ (1.39$\times$, all violations${\to}$0\%).
Per-beam memory overhead is $O(k \times |\text{entities}| \times |\text{types}|)$ for independent entity registry copies, negligible at typical document scales.

\paragraph{70B-class validation (single-family).}
\label{sec:70b-results}
The following results constitute a single-family scale validation on Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct (AWQ INT4); cross-family verification (e.g., Qwen-72B) remains future work.
All 70B experiments use Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct under AWQ INT4 quantization; an 8B ablation confirms constraint enforcement is unaffected by quantization (Appendix~\ref{app:quantization}).
Zero-shot S1 eliminates DR on both datasets (SciERC 6.41\%\,$\to$\,0\%, DocRED 14.98\%\,$\to$\,0\%; R-F1 11--13).
% exp_ids: r16_70b_scierc_zs_ablation (grammar_only, semantic_only, full_s1)
A four-way ablation reveals scale-dependent layer interaction: semantic-only achieves 84\% DR reduction vs.\ 8B's 24\% (Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation}), though grammar remains necessary for RV elimination and CF control (semantic-only CF${=}$76).
% exp_ids: eval_70b_lora_scierc_s1_constrained, eval_70b_lora_docred_200_s1_constrained
LoRA confirms composability: DR\,$\to$\,0\% on both datasets (R-F1 44.53, 43.95; $|\Delta| \leq 0.20$\,pp; CF 0.18--1.33\%); cross-family generalization at 70B scale remains to be verified.
% exp_ids: eval_70b_lora_docred_200_beam4_s1
Beam ($k{=}4$) reduces DocRED parse failures (12.5\%\,$\to$\,0.5\%, R-F1 $+$4.19\,pp); SciERC controlled comparison isolates pure beam gain at $+$0.28\,pp (Appendix~\ref{app:70b-ablation}).

% exp_ids: trie_qwen_ft_scierc, trie_qwen_zs_scierc, trie_llama_ft_scierc, trie_llama_zs_scierc
\paragraph{Comparison with grammar-constrained approaches.}
\label{sec:constrained-baselines}
Our grammar-only ablation (Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation}, row~2) implements the same constraints as GCD~\cite{geng2023gcd} and BoostCD~\cite{boostcd2025}; vLLM \texttt{guided\_json}~\cite{kwon2023vllm} confirms equivalence on Qwen3-8B (DR${=}$15.26\%; other models use the same backend; Appendix~\ref{app:gcd-comparison}).
The ${\sim}$15\% residual DR is the gap our semantic layer addresses (94\% total reduction); trie-only constraints without JSON enforcement yield 9--51\% parse failure (Appendix~\ref{app:trie-baseline}).

\begin{abstract}
Large language models for information extraction generate structurally valid but ontologically invalid triples---where entity types violate the ontology's domain/range constraints.
These violations persist across the capability spectrum and cannot be addressed by grammar-constrained decoding (which lacks cross-field type awareness) or post-hoc filtering (which discards valid predictions).

We present \textsc{OntoCoDec}, a framework that compiles information extraction ontologies into composable token-level decoding constraints.
A decidability analysis shows that domain/range constraints exceed context-free expressiveness, yielding a two-layer architecture: a grammar layer enforces structural validity and vocabulary membership; a semantic layer enforces type constraints at runtime through stateful masking over a dynamic entity registry, with grammar-first fallback when constraints conflict.

% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates follow an observed pattern consistent with schema restrictiveness (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
At competitive quality (R-F1 41--47\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering discards up to 48\% of predictions including true positives (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} compiles ontology constraints into context-free grammars (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} interprets type constraints at runtime via dynamic logit masking over an entity registry, with a scale-dependent layer interaction: at 8B, the semantic layer achieves only 24\% independent DR reduction (near-complete when combined), while at 70B it reaches 84\% independently.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies, requires no constraint-specific training, and is applicable to autoregressive LMs with logits access; we validate on three English datasets (up to 96 relation types), three 8B-class models across three tokenizer families, with 70B-class validation (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
LoRA + greedy S1 achieves near-complete DR elimination: DR\,$\leq$\,0.09\% at R-F1 41--47\% ($\pm$0.8\,pp, $+$10\% latency); beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types on both RE datasets under fine-tuning (1.39$\times$ latency).
DR enforcement converts ontologically invalid violations to individually valid but type-inconsistent ones (CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\% fine-tuned); zero-shot DR drops 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED, with total violations decreasing $\sim$31\% (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).

OntoCoDec is a constraint enforcement method, orthogonal and complementary to training-based schema-aware approaches such as GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie} and KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}; it can be composed with any generative IE system to improve schema compliance without retraining.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item A two-layer constrained decoding framework, formalizing a known intuition for the IE setting: that domain/range type constraints require stateful enforcement beyond context-free grammars (Proposition~1), yielding pair-based sequential enforcement (\S\ref{sec:decidability}). Constraints compile automatically from IE ontologies, validated on schemas with up to 96 relation types.
    \item Systematic ablation across 3 model families (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B) and 2 datasets (SciERC, DocRED) under both zero-shot and LoRA fine-tuned settings, demonstrating DR elimination ($\leq$0.09\%) with R-F1 within $\pm$0.8\,pp; DR enforcement introduces CF as a correctable side effect (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}); a preliminary $n{=}20$ event extraction pilot provides directional evidence of task generalization (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}).
    \item Single-family scale validation on Llama-3.1-70B (AWQ INT4), revealing a scale-dependent layer interaction: the semantic layer alone achieves 84\% DR reduction at 70B vs.\ 24\% at 8B (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}). Beam $k{=}2$ is Pareto-optimal (R-F1 44.60, CF 0.11\%, 1.18$\times$ latency); $k{=}4$ eliminates all violations at 1.39$\times$.
\end{enumerate}

% Section 7 — Discussion and Conclusion

OntoCoDec compiles IE ontologies into composable token-level constraints, validated across 3 datasets, 3+ models, and 2 tasks.
Because IE type constraints exceed context-free expressiveness (Proposition~1), the semantic layer bridges the gap grammar-only enforcement cannot address (3\% vs.\ 94\% DR reduction at 8B), using constructive forward masking over a dynamic entity registry.
This scale-dependent interaction (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}) suggests grammar-constrained decoding is necessary but increasingly insufficient as models improve; constraint enforcement is preserved under INT4 quantization (4$\times$ compression; Appendix~\ref{app:quantization}).

\paragraph{DR$\leftrightarrow$CF trade-off.}
Greedy S1 reduces DR to ${<}$0.1\% but introduces CF (zero-shot $+$9.82\,pp, fine-tuned $+$1.18\,pp)---an architectural consequence of per-triple independent enforcement, where first-seen type registration (\S\ref{sec:entity-registry}) may conflict with subsequent requirements.
Beam search mitigates this: $k{=}2$ reduces CF to 0.11\% at 1.18$\times$ latency (Pareto-optimal); $k{=}4$ eliminates all CF at 1.39$\times$ (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
The trade-off is a net severity downgrade: DR is irrecoverable, while CF is amenable to post-hoc resolution (TCR eliminates 18--92\%; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).

\paragraph{Complementarity with training-based enforcement.}
GoLLIE and KnowCoder internalize schema knowledge via training but cannot guarantee runtime compliance; OntoCoDec provides a complementary runtime guarantee layer.
LoRA + S1 validates this: training reduces DR to 1--2\%, constraints eliminate the residual; neither alone achieves both high R-F1 and near-zero DR.

\paragraph{Per-triple vs.\ global enforcement.}
Per-triple enforcement cannot coordinate cross-triple type assignments---the source of CF violations (Level~3 non-local constraints; \S\ref{sec:decidability}).
Global enforcement requires entity-level type consensus across the full output, exceeding online per-token masking; beam search approximates this, TCR provides post-hoc correction, and integrating entity-level consensus into the decoding loop remains future work.

\paragraph{Zero-shot diagnostic.}
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: DR=0.1537; phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093
Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation} establishes that DR violations are pervasive (15--18\% across datasets) and that constraint layers interact non-additively: grammar-only achieves 3\% DR reduction on SciERC, semantic-only 24\%, but their composition yields 94\%---the \emph{empirical enabling dependency}.
On DocRED (96 relations, $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$), grammar-only \emph{increases} DR via \textit{latent violation surfacing}: forcing OOV$\to$valid relation mapping exposes violations previously masked by vocabulary errors (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).
Cross-model validation (3 models $\times$ 2 datasets; Table~\ref{tab:cross-model}) confirms DR drops of 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED, with R-F1 improving in 5/6 settings; post-hoc filtering achieves DR${=}$0\% but at 15--74\% rejection rates.
DR-to-CF conversion represents a severity downgrade: DR is irrecoverable without re-extraction, while CF---individually valid triples with cross-triple inconsistency---is amenable to post-hoc resolution (TCR eliminates 18--92\%; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).

\label{sec:composability}

Under fine-tuning, grammar becomes a no-op ($\Delta$DR$<$0.2\,pp), making the semantic layer the sole DR defense (39--69\% reduction; Appendix~\ref{app:ft-ablation}); three relations with $\kappa \geq 0.36$ retain DR, all eliminated by S1 (Appendix~\ref{app:lora-per-relation}).
Fallback frequency is model-dependent: Qwen triggers 0 fallbacks under LoRA + S1 on SciERC, while Llama triggers 5{,}882 (Table~\ref{tab:ft-ablation}), reflecting weaker entity typing; despite this, DR reaches 0.09\% for Llama, confirming that even frequent fallback does not compromise enforcement.
CF drops from $+$9.82\,pp (zero-shot) to $+$1.18\,pp (fine-tuned), concentrated in \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X ambiguity (63.3\% of zero-shot CF; Appendix~\ref{app:cf-distribution}); beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types (R-F1 43--47; \S\ref{sec:beam-results}).

% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_full_s1 (ZS: CF=248, 167 docs), w5_lora_scierc_full_s1_eval (FT: CF=22, 20 docs)
Under zero-shot greedy S1, CF is the sole residual violation type (DR, RV, ET all eliminated): 248 cross-field violations arise across 167 documents, of which 63.3\% involve \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X type ambiguity (Appendix~\ref{app:cf-distribution}), concentrated in \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$\textsc{OtherScientificTerm} (34.7\%) and \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$\textsc{Material} (12.3\%).

\begin{abstract}
Large language models for information extraction generate structurally valid but ontologically invalid triples---where entity types violate the ontology's domain/range constraints.
These violations persist across the capability spectrum and cannot be addressed by grammar-constrained decoding (which lacks cross-field type awareness) or post-hoc filtering (which discards valid predictions).

We present \textsc{OntoCoDec}, a framework that compiles information extraction ontologies into composable token-level decoding constraints.
A decidability analysis shows that domain/range constraints exceed context-free expressiveness, yielding a two-layer architecture: a grammar layer enforces structural validity and vocabulary membership; a semantic layer enforces type constraints at runtime through stateful masking over a dynamic entity registry, with grammar-first fallback when constraints conflict.

In zero-shot settings, cross-field rates are higher (up to 12\%) but decrease with model calibration.

\end{abstract}

% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates follow an observed pattern consistent with schema restrictiveness (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
At competitive quality (R-F1 41--47\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering discards up to 48\% of predictions including true positives (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} compiles ontology constraints into context-free grammars (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} interprets type constraints at runtime via dynamic logit masking over an entity registry, with a scale-dependent layer interaction: at 8B, the semantic layer achieves only 24\% independent DR reduction (near-complete when combined), while at 70B it reaches 84\% independently.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies, requires no constraint-specific training, and is applicable to autoregressive LMs with logits access; we validate on three English datasets (up to 96 relation types), three 8B-class models across three tokenizer families, with 70B-class validation (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
LoRA + greedy S1 reduces DR to near-zero: DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\% at R-F1 41--46\% ($\pm$0.3\,pp, $+$10\% latency); beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types on both RE datasets under fine-tuning (1.39$\times$ latency).
DR enforcement converts ontologically invalid violations to individually valid but type-inconsistent ones (CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\% fine-tuned); zero-shot DR drops 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED, with total violations decreasing $\sim$31\% (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).

OntoCoDec is a constraint enforcement method, orthogonal and complementary to training-based schema-aware approaches such as GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie} and KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}; it can be composed with any generative IE system to improve schema compliance without retraining.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item A two-layer constrained decoding framework, formalizing a known intuition for the IE setting: that domain/range type constraints require stateful enforcement beyond context-free grammars (Proposition~1), yielding pair-based sequential enforcement (\S\ref{sec:decidability}). Constraints compile automatically from IE ontologies, validated on schemas with up to 96 relation types.
    \item Systematic ablation across 3 model families (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B) and 2 datasets (SciERC, DocRED) under both zero-shot and LoRA fine-tuned settings, demonstrating DR elimination ($\leq$0.09\%) with R-F1 within $\pm$0.8\,pp; DR enforcement introduces CF as a correctable side effect (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}); a preliminary $n{=}20$ event extraction pilot provides directional evidence of task generalization (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}).
    \item Single-family scale validation on Llama-3.1-70B (AWQ INT4), revealing a scale-dependent layer interaction: the semantic layer alone achieves 84\% DR reduction at 70B vs.\ 24\% at 8B (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}). Beam $k{=}2$ is Pareto-optimal (R-F1 44.60, CF 0.11\%, 1.18$\times$ latency); $k{=}4$ eliminates all violations at 1.39$\times$.
\end{enumerate}

\label{sec:violation_landscape}

We evaluate OntoCoDec in two deployment configurations: greedy S1 (DR\,$\leq$\,0.09\%, $+$10\% latency) and beam S1 (all violations\,$\to$\,0\%, 1.39$\times$ latency); zero-shot evaluation (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}) serves as a diagnostic probe for the fine-tuned setting (R-F1 41--47\%).

\paragraph{Setup.}
We evaluate on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} (551 test sentences, 7 relations, $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$) and DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} (998 dev documents,\footnote{DocRED test annotations are not publicly available; we evaluate on the development set.} 96 relations, $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$).
RE type constraints are extracted from observed type pairs in training data (neither dataset provides a formal ontology); EE constraints on WikiEvents (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}) derive from the KAIROS ontology.
All constraints are schema-level, independent of evaluation splits.
Primary model: Qwen3-8B~\cite{qwen2025qwen3}, zero-shot greedy decoding; cross-model validation in Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}, composability with fine-tuning in \S\ref{sec:composability}.
LoRA hyperparameters (rank, $\alpha$, learning rate) were tuned on SciERC and transferred to DocRED without dataset-specific optimization; given the substantial schema complexity difference (7 vs.\ 96 relations), this transfer may underestimate DocRED fine-tuning potential.
Our R-F1 range (41--47\% under LoRA) is consistent with recent LLM-based generative RE evaluations on these benchmarks, where document-level closed IE without gold entity spans typically achieves 35--50\%~\cite{wadhwa2023revisiting}; supervised span-based methods operating under different assumptions (gold entity spans, dedicated architectures) are not directly comparable.
DocRED development documents were used for evaluation only.
Four violation categories: \textbf{DR} (type pair $\notin \sigma(r)$), \textbf{RV} (relation $\notin \mathcal{R}$), \textbf{ET} (entity type $\notin \mathcal{E}$), \textbf{CF} (conflicting types across triples).
Baseline DR: 15.37\% (SciERC), 18.46\% (DocRED); schema-informed prompting reduces DR by 62\% but is per-relation unreliable (Appendix~\ref{app:per-relation-landscape}).

% §5 Setup (compressed from Violation Landscape)
% exp_ids: mvp_phase0_violation_rate, mvp_phase0_scierc_schema,
%          mvp_phase0_violation_rate_docred, mvp_phase0_docred_schema

\label{sec:violation_landscape}

We evaluate OntoCoDec in two deployment configurations: greedy S1 (DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\%, $+$10\% latency) and beam S1 (all violations\,$\to$\,0\%, 1.39$\times$ latency); zero-shot evaluation (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}) serves as a diagnostic probe for the fine-tuned setting (R-F1 41--46\%).

\paragraph{Setup.}
We evaluate on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} (551 test sentences, 7 relations, $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$) and DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} (998 dev documents,\footnote{DocRED test annotations are not publicly available; we evaluate on the development set.} 96 relations, $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$).
RE type constraints are extracted from observed type pairs in training data (neither dataset provides a formal ontology); EE constraints on WikiEvents (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}) derive from the KAIROS ontology.
All constraints are schema-level, independent of evaluation splits.
Primary model: Qwen3-8B~\cite{qwen2025qwen3}, zero-shot greedy decoding; cross-model validation in Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}, composability with fine-tuning in \S\ref{sec:composability}.
LoRA hyperparameters (rank, $\alpha$, learning rate) were tuned on SciERC and transferred to DocRED without dataset-specific optimization; given the substantial schema complexity difference (7 vs.\ 96 relations), this transfer may underestimate DocRED fine-tuning potential.
Our R-F1 range (41--47\% under LoRA) is consistent with recent LLM-based generative RE evaluations on these benchmarks, where document-level closed IE without gold entity spans typically achieves 35--50\%~\cite{wadhwa2023revisiting}; supervised span-based methods operating under different assumptions (gold entity spans, dedicated architectures) are not directly comparable.
DocRED development documents were used for evaluation only.
Four violation categories: \textbf{DR} (type pair $\notin \sigma(r)$), \textbf{RV} (relation $\notin \mathcal{R}$), \textbf{ET} (entity type $\notin \mathcal{E}$), \textbf{CF} (conflicting types across triples).
Baseline DR: 15.37\% (SciERC), 18.46\% (DocRED); schema-informed prompting reduces DR by 62\% but is per-relation unreliable (Appendix~\ref{app:per-relation-landscape}).

% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates follow an observed pattern consistent with schema restrictiveness (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
At competitive quality (R-F1 41--47\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering discards up to 48\% of predictions including true positives (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} compiles ontology constraints into context-free grammars (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} interprets type constraints at runtime via dynamic logit masking over an entity registry, with a scale-dependent layer interaction: at 8B, the semantic layer achieves only 24\% independent DR reduction (near-complete when combined), while at 70B it reaches 84\% independently.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies, requires no constraint-specific training, and is applicable to autoregressive LMs with logits access; we validate on three English datasets (up to 96 relation types), three 8B-class models across three tokenizer families, with 70B-class validation (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
LoRA + greedy S1 reduces DR to near-zero: DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\% at R-F1 41--46\% ($\pm$0.3\,pp, $+$10\% latency); beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types on both RE datasets under fine-tuning (1.39$\times$ latency).
DR enforcement converts ontologically invalid violations to individually valid but type-inconsistent ones (CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\% fine-tuned); zero-shot DR drops 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED, with total violations decreasing $\sim$31\% (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).

OntoCoDec is a constraint enforcement method, orthogonal and complementary to training-based schema-aware approaches such as GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie} and KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}; it can be composed with any generative IE system to improve schema compliance without retraining.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item A two-layer constrained decoding framework, formalizing a known intuition for the IE setting: that domain/range type constraints require stateful enforcement beyond context-free grammars (Proposition~1), yielding pair-based sequential enforcement (\S\ref{sec:decidability}). Constraints compile automatically from IE ontologies, validated on schemas with up to 96 relation types.
    \item Systematic ablation across 3 model families (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B) and 2 datasets (SciERC, DocRED) under both zero-shot and LoRA fine-tuned settings, demonstrating DR reduction to $\leq$0.21\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.3\,pp; DR enforcement introduces CF as a correctable side effect (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}); a preliminary $n{=}20$ event extraction pilot provides directional evidence of task generalization (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}).
    \item Single-family scale validation on Llama-3.1-70B (AWQ INT4), revealing a scale-dependent layer interaction: the semantic layer alone achieves 84\% DR reduction at 70B vs.\ 24\% at 8B (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}). Beam $k{=}2$ is Pareto-optimal (R-F1 44.60, CF 0.11\%, 1.18$\times$ latency); $k{=}4$ eliminates all violations at 1.39$\times$.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{abstract}
Large language models for information extraction generate structurally valid but ontologically invalid triples---where entity types violate the ontology's domain/range constraints.
These violations persist across the capability spectrum and cannot be addressed by grammar-constrained decoding (which lacks cross-field type awareness) or post-hoc filtering (which discards valid predictions).

We present \textsc{OntoCoDec}, a framework that compiles information extraction ontologies into composable token-level decoding constraints.
A decidability analysis shows that domain/range constraints exceed context-free expressiveness, yielding a two-layer architecture: a grammar layer enforces structural validity and vocabulary membership; a semantic layer enforces type constraints at runtime through stateful masking over a dynamic entity registry, with grammar-first fallback when constraints conflict.

Evaluated across three 8B-class models and two relation extraction datasets (up to 96 relations), OntoCoDec composed with LoRA fine-tuning reduces domain/range violations to near-zero ($\leq$\,0.21\%) at F1 41--46\%, but introduces cross-field type inconsistencies ($\leq$1.4\%) as the dominant residual---an architectural consequence of per-triple independent enforcement.
Beam search ($k{=}2$) reduces CF to 0.11\% at 1.18$\times$ latency; $k{=}4$ eliminates all violation types at 1.39$\times$.
In zero-shot settings, cross-field rates are higher (up to 12\%) but decrease with model calibration.
Zero-shot domain/range reductions span 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED; violation rates follow an observed pattern consistent with schema restrictiveness across our three evaluation schemas ($n{=}3$; insufficient for statistical inference), with a scale-dependent relationship between the two layers.
\end{abstract}

\paragraph{Zero-shot diagnostic.}
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: DR=0.1537; phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093
Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation} establishes that DR violations are pervasive (15--18\% across datasets) and that constraint layers interact non-additively: grammar-only achieves 3\% DR reduction on SciERC, semantic-only 24\%, but their composition yields 94\%---the \emph{empirical enabling dependency}.
On DocRED (96 relations, $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$), grammar-only \emph{increases} DR via \textit{latent violation surfacing}: forcing OOV$\to$valid relation mapping exposes violations previously masked by vocabulary errors (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).
Cross-model validation (3 models $\times$ 2 datasets; Table~\ref{tab:cross-model}) confirms DR drops of 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED, with R-F1 improving in 5/6 settings; post-hoc filtering achieves DR${=}$0\% but at 15--74\% rejection rates.
DR-to-CF conversion represents a severity downgrade: DR is irrecoverable without re-extraction, while CF---individually valid triples with cross-triple inconsistency---is amenable to post-hoc resolution (TCR eliminates 18--92\%; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).
Zero-shot evaluation thus establishes violation prevalence and constraint interaction; fine-tuning demonstrates practical elimination.

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (e) Composability with Fine-Tuning (expanded)
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
\label{sec:composability}
% exp_ids: bootstrap_ci_ft_composability.json, w5_lora_scierc_*, w8_*
Fine-tuning alone reduces DR to 1--2\% but leaves residual violations on tight-constraint relations (Table~\ref{tab:composability}); adding S1 yields DR\,$\leq$\,0.09\% with no significant $\Delta$R-F1 (Bonferroni-corrected; 95\% CIs $\subseteq [-0.69, {+}0.25]$\,pp; removed triples are 97.6--100\% false positives; Appendix~\ref{app:downstream-impact}).

1	% Section 7 — Discussion and Conclusion
2	
3	OntoCoDec compiles IE ontologies into composable token-level constraints, validated across 3 datasets, 3+ models, and 2 tasks.
4	Because IE type constraints exceed context-free expressiveness (Proposition~1), the semantic layer bridges the gap grammar-only enforcement cannot address (3\% vs.\ 94\% DR reduction at 8B), using constructive forward masking over a dynamic entity registry.
5	This scale-dependent interaction (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}) suggests grammar-constrained decoding is necessary but increasingly insufficient as models improve; constraint enforcement is preserved under INT4 quantization (4$\times$ compression; Appendix~\ref{app:quantization}).
6	
7	\paragraph{DR$\leftrightarrow$CF trade-off.}
8	Greedy S1 reduces DR to ${<}$0.1\% but introduces CF (zero-shot $+$9.82\,pp, fine-tuned $+$1.18\,pp)---an architectural consequence of per-triple independent enforcement, where first-seen type registration (\S\ref{sec:entity-registry}) may conflict with subsequent requirements.
9	Beam search mitigates this: $k{=}2$ reduces CF to 0.11\% at 1.18$\times$ latency (Pareto-optimal); $k{=}4$ eliminates all CF at 1.39$\times$ (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
10	The trade-off is a net severity downgrade: DR is irrecoverable, while CF is amenable to post-hoc resolution (TCR eliminates 18--92\%; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).
11	
12	\paragraph{Complementarity with training-based enforcement.}
13	GoLLIE and KnowCoder internalize schema knowledge via training but cannot guarantee runtime compliance; OntoCoDec provides a complementary runtime guarantee layer.
14	LoRA + S1 validates this: training reduces DR to 1--2\%, constraints eliminate the residual; neither alone achieves both high R-F1 and near-zero DR.
15	
16	\paragraph{Per-triple vs.\ global enforcement.}
17	Per-triple enforcement cannot coordinate cross-triple type assignments---the source of CF violations (Level~3 non-local constraints; \S\ref{sec:decidability}).
18	Global enforcement requires entity-level type consensus across the full output, exceeding online per-token masking; beam search approximates this, TCR provides post-hoc correction, and integrating entity-level consensus into the decoding loop remains future work.

% Section 7 — Discussion and Conclusion

OntoCoDec compiles IE ontologies into composable token-level constraints, validated across 3 datasets, 3+ models, and 2 tasks.
Because IE type constraints exceed context-free expressiveness (Proposition~1), the semantic layer bridges the gap grammar-only enforcement cannot address (3\% vs.\ 94\% DR reduction at 8B), using constructive forward masking over a dynamic entity registry.
This scale-dependent interaction (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}) suggests grammar-constrained decoding is necessary but increasingly insufficient as models improve; constraint enforcement is preserved under INT4 quantization (4$\times$ compression; Appendix~\ref{app:quantization}).

\paragraph{DR$\leftrightarrow$CF trade-off.}
Greedy S1 reduces DR to ${<}$0.1\% but introduces CF (zero-shot $+$9.82\,pp, fine-tuned $+$1.18\,pp)---an architectural consequence of per-triple independent enforcement, where first-seen type registration (\S\ref{sec:entity-registry}) may conflict with subsequent requirements.
Beam search mitigates this: $k{=}2$ reduces CF to 0.11\% at 1.18$\times$ latency (Pareto-optimal); $k{=}4$ eliminates all CF at 1.39$\times$ (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
The trade-off is a net severity downgrade: DR is irrecoverable, while CF is amenable to post-hoc resolution (TCR eliminates 18--92\%; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).

\paragraph{Complementarity with training-based enforcement.}
GoLLIE and KnowCoder internalize schema knowledge via training but cannot guarantee runtime compliance; OntoCoDec provides a complementary runtime guarantee layer.
LoRA + S1 validates this: training reduces DR to 1--2\%, constraints eliminate the residual; neither alone achieves both high R-F1 and near-zero DR.

\paragraph{Per-triple vs.\ global enforcement.}
Per-triple enforcement cannot coordinate cross-triple type assignments---the source of CF violations (Level~3 non-local constraints; \S\ref{sec:decidability}).
Global enforcement requires entity-level type consensus across the full output, exceeding online per-token masking; beam search approximates this, TCR provides post-hoc correction, and integrating entity-level consensus into the decoding loop remains future work.

\paragraph{Residual DR Error Analysis.}
\label{app:residual-dr-analysis}

Across all fine-tuned settings (2 models $\times$ 2 datasets $\times$ S1), only 36 domain/range violations remain.
Manual inspection reveals four root causes:

\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item \emph{Entity type errors} (39\%): the LLM assigns an incorrect entity type (e.g., labeling a geographic entity as \textsc{LOC} when the gold standard requires \textsc{MISC}), causing the semantic mask to permit a domain/range-incompatible relation.
\item \emph{Schema coverage gaps} (33\%): the frequency-based constraint table, constructed from training-set co-occurrence statistics, does not cover long-tail type pairs that are ontologically valid but rare. These violations are irreducible by decoding-time constraints alone.
\item \emph{Incorrect relation selection} (17\%): the model selects a semantically inappropriate relation whose domain/range constraints are incompatible with the correctly typed entities.
\item \emph{Direction reversal} (11\%): the model assigns the correct relation but inverts head/tail roles, placing entities in positions that violate the relation's asymmetric domain/range specification.
\end{enumerate}

Two dataset-specific patterns emerge.
Outside Llama DocRED, all residual violations (3 of 36, spanning Llama SciERC and Qwen DocRED) trace exclusively to schema coverage gaps: the model's entity typing is accurate, and the constraint system has reached its theoretical ceiling given the frequency-based constraint table.
On DocRED, Llama-3.1-8B contributes 33 of 36 residual violations (92\%), with entity type errors as the dominant cause (14/33, 42\%).
This asymmetry reflects Llama's weaker fine-tuned entity typing on DocRED's larger ontology (96 relations, 6 entity types) compared to Qwen, which achieves near-zero residual.
The implication is twofold: (i)~the irreducible floor from schema gaps is small ($\sim$3 violations across 4 settings), so the constraint system operates near its theoretical optimum; (ii)~residual violations from entity typing errors are addressable through stronger base models or improved entity typing modules, without modifying the constraint architecture.

70	\paragraph{Constraint scope.}
71	CF is an architectural consequence of per-triple independent enforcement: CF$\leftrightarrow$DR represents a fundamental trade-off (eliminating CF re-routes violations to DR; Appendix~\ref{app:cf-dr-tradeoff}), and its impact is model-dependent (S1 introduces CF for calibrated models but reduces it for poorly-calibrated ones).
72	Global entity-level type consensus during decoding offers the most direct path to resolving CF.
73	Entity-first generation order is an architectural constraint: the grammar enforces entities before relations, ensuring the registry is populated before type checks; alternative orderings would require deferred constraint evaluation.
74	Residual DR under fine-tuning (36 violations total) decomposes into entity type errors (39\%), schema coverage gaps (33\%), and model generation errors (28\%); schema gaps arise from training-data-derived constraints that may not cover all valid type pairs (Appendix~\ref{app:residual-dr-analysis}).
75	We do not decompose CF violations into first-seen cascading errors versus legitimate type ambiguity; this decomposition requires gold entity type annotations at the mention level, which SciERC provides only at the entity level.
76	Post-hoc type consensus re-voting reduces CF by 18--92\% (Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}), but integrating consensus into the decoding loop remains future work.
77	
78	\paragraph{Evaluation coverage.}
79	Zero-shot evaluation covers three 8B-class and one 70B-class model; fine-tuning composability is validated on two 8B-class models (full datasets) and one 70B-class model (SciERC full, DocRED 200-document subset).

Entity-first generation order is an architectural constraint: the grammar enforces entities before relations, ensuring the registry is populated before type checks; alternative orderings would require deferred constraint evaluation.
Residual DR under fine-tuning (36 violations total) decomposes into entity type errors (39\%), schema coverage gaps (33\%), and model generation errors (28\%); schema gaps arise from training-data-derived constraints that may not cover all valid type pairs (Appendix~\ref{app:residual-dr-analysis}).
We do not decompose CF violations into first-seen cascading errors versus legitimate type ambiguity; this decomposition requires gold entity type annotations at the mention level, which SciERC provides only at the entity level.
Post-hoc type consensus re-voting reduces CF by 18--92\% (Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}), but integrating consensus into the decoding loop remains future work.

Zero-shot evaluation covers three 8B-class and one 70B-class model; fine-tuning composability is validated on two 8B-class models (full datasets) and one 70B-class model (SciERC full, DocRED 200-document subset).

% Runtime overhead (inline paragraph, no subsection header to save space)

\paragraph{Runtime overhead.}
\label{sec:runtime}
S1 overhead is $+$13.1\% on SciERC, lower on DocRED due to amortization over longer sequences; under LoRA, $+$10.0\% with 37\% lower absolute latency.
Constraint compilation is one-time $<$0.5\,s; scaling benchmarks confirm constant overhead (2--3\%) up to 200 entity types and 1{,}000 relations (Appendix~\ref{app:scalability}).

\paragraph{Beam search compatibility.}
\label{sec:beam-results}
% exp_id: d066_beam_sweep
With LoRA, beam search~\cite{anderson2017guided} eliminates all four violation types on both SciERC and DocRED at both 8B and 70B scales (Appendix~\ref{app:beam-search}).
A beam-width sweep ($k \in \{1,2,4,8\}$) on SciERC reveals $k{=}2$ as Pareto-optimal: R-F1 44.60 (highest), CF 0.11\%, at only 1.18$\times$ greedy S1 latency; $k{=}4$ achieves CF${=}$0\% but lower R-F1 (43.60) at 1.39$\times$ (Table~\ref{tab:beam-sweep}; latencies relative to greedy S1).
This yields three deployment tiers: greedy S1 ($+$10\% latency, DR${<}$0.1\%, CF${\leq}$1.4\%), beam $k{=}2$ (1.18$\times$, near-zero CF), and beam $k{=}4$ (1.39$\times$, all violations${\to}$0\%).
Per-beam memory overhead is $O(k \times |\text{entities}| \times |\text{types}|)$ for independent entity registry copies, negligible at typical document scales.

% exp_ids: r16_70b_scierc_zs_s1, r16_70b_docred_zs_s1, 70b_lora_scierc, 70b_lora_docred_200
\paragraph{70B-class validation (single-family).}
\label{sec:70b-results}
The following results constitute a single-family scale validation on Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct (AWQ INT4); cross-family verification (e.g., Qwen-72B) remains future work.
All 70B experiments use Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct under AWQ INT4 quantization; an 8B ablation confirms constraint enforcement is unaffected by quantization (Appendix~\ref{app:quantization}).
Zero-shot S1 eliminates DR on both datasets (SciERC 6.41\%\,$\to$\,0\%, DocRED 14.98\%\,$\to$\,0\%; R-F1 11--13).
% exp_ids: r16_70b_scierc_zs_ablation (grammar_only, semantic_only, full_s1)
A four-way ablation reveals scale-dependent layer interaction: semantic-only achieves 84\% DR reduction vs.\ 8B's 24\% (Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation}), though grammar remains necessary for RV elimination and CF control (semantic-only CF${=}$76).
% exp_ids: eval_70b_lora_scierc_s1_constrained, eval_70b_lora_docred_200_s1_constrained
LoRA confirms composability: DR\,$\to$\,0\% on both datasets (R-F1 44.53, 43.95; $|\Delta| \leq 0.20$\,pp; CF 0.18--1.33\%); cross-family generalization at 70B scale remains to be verified.
% exp_ids: eval_70b_lora_docred_200_beam4_s1
Beam ($k{=}4$) reduces DocRED parse failures (12.5\%\,$\to$\,0.5\%, R-F1 $+$4.19\,pp); SciERC controlled comparison isolates pure beam gain at $+$0.28\,pp (Appendix~\ref{app:70b-ablation}).

% exp_ids: trie_qwen_ft_scierc, trie_qwen_zs_scierc, trie_llama_ft_scierc, trie_llama_zs_scierc
\paragraph{Comparison with grammar-constrained approaches.}
\label{sec:constrained-baselines}
Our grammar-only ablation (Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation}, row~2) implements the same constraints as GCD~\cite{geng2023gcd} and BoostCD~\cite{boostcd2025}; vLLM \texttt{guided\_json}~\cite{kwon2023vllm} confirms equivalence on Qwen3-8B (DR${=}$15.26\%; other models use the same backend; Appendix~\ref{app:gcd-comparison}).
The ${\sim}$15\% residual DR is the gap our semantic layer addresses (94\% total reduction); trie-only constraints without JSON enforcement yield 9--51\% parse failure (Appendix~\ref{app:trie-baseline}).
